payload.text: More money, fewer rounds. That, in short, is the state of U.S. Series B startup funding in 2026, as venture capital investment continues to concentrate heavily around a handful of AI hotshots. Crunchbase data shows that so far this year, investors have poured around $48 billion into financings around the Series B stage 1 , the highest tally in years. Yet round counts are below year-ago levels and are on track for a multiyear low. Smaller Series B rounds grow scarcer One trend driving capital concentration is a sharp decline in small and mid-sized Series B rounds. So far this year, less than a third of deals in our sample set 2 were for under $30 million. By contrast, between 2021 and 2025, rounds in this range accounted for about half of deals, per Crunchbase data. The smallest Series B deals have gotten particularly scarce. This year there were just 26 rounds under $10 million in our sample set. Big rounds still a big thing On the flip side, really large Series B rounds are quite popular. At least 110 companies have raised rounds of $100 million or more around this stage so far this year. That’s roughly a quarter of all deals. Of these, the largest by far was a $12 billion round 3 for Prometheus , Jeff Bezos ’ physical AI startup that launched last year. Model developer World Labs , led by AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li , was tied for next-biggest fundraiser, closing on $1 billion in February. Nuclear energy startup Valar Atomics also secured $1 billion in Series B funding across tranches this year, with Sequoia Capital as lead investor. For  a wider snapshot, below we put together a sample list of more of this year’s biggest U.S. Series B recipients. Mostly an AI story Meanwhile, one of the least surprising findings from our analysis of Series B recipients is that it was a heavily AI-focused group. So far this year, about two-thirds of Series B funding has gone to AI-focused startups, per Crunchbase data. In 2025, by comparison, about half of investment went to companies in AI categories. AI companies were also heavily represented by round count. So far in 2026, more than half of all reported U.S. Series B deals have been for AI companies. Bullish climate for Series B Overall, the numbers point to a bullish climate for Series B investment, particularly for AI startups with demonstrated traction. The environment looks particularly favorable for companies that have already raised considerable sums at Series A and seed. Even so, these don’t look like the best of times for startups seeking smaller Series B rounds. Seems like in the current AI-driven cycle, investors are increasingly focused on big checks for high-valuation companies. For most seed founders, that headline is a warning. U.S. startups closed 272 Series A rounds in the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data, about 28% fewer than the 377 a year earlier. Seed held up better, at 984 rounds vs. 1,059. The megarounds hide how few A rounds are getting done. Seed checks keep growing. The median U.S. seed round was about $3 million last year, 3x its 2018 level, according to Crunchbase . Yet only 24% of companies that raised a $1 million-plus seed in 2023 have moved past seed, and just 16% of the 2024 cohort, down from 55% or higher through 2020. Size your seed against the Series A Uncork Capital ‘s Andy McLoughlin told Crunchbase News that Series A investors now expect $2 million to $3 million in ARR, sometimes $4 million, and the time from seed to A has stretched past two years. If a seed won’t carry you to that bar with six months to spare, a smaller round is the better deal. A bigger seed isn’t required. Take Atomic , a New York-based supply chain planning software company founded in 2023 (and not an MGV portfolio company). It raised a $3 million seed , right at the median, in April 2025, led by Madrona and DVx Ventures , then closed a $12.5 million Series A led by Madrona and Klass Capital about 17 months later. Map your Series A leads now Funds of $100 million to $500 million typically lead the Series A. Figure out which ones lead at your stage and when their current fund closes, then send the right partners updates for a year before you ask for anything. Sell your way to the bar The Series A bar is now a revenue bar, which makes it a go-to-market problem first. Most seed companies I meet have a stronger product than sales motion. At MGV, our work starts with a first session we call Sales Jumpstart: we interview the founders and their team. We then score the company on our proprietary matrix: where it is today, where it should be, and what it needs to become a scalable go-to-market machine. From there, founders work through workshops on outbound reach, qualification, profiling, the funnel, objection handling, hiring assessment, compensation plans, fundraising, deck building, storytelling and investor intros, with mentoring alongside. A company at $2 million in ARR with a sales process a new hire can run is a better Series A candidate than one at $3 million built on founder-led deals nobody else can repeat. The founders who make it are already planning for the round after this one. As the co-founder and managing partner of MGV , Marc Schröder is committed to establishing MGV as the premier venture firm for world-class tech entrepreneurs to accelerate their visions. Under Schröder’s stewardship, MGV has swiftly ascended to a top-quartile firm, surpassing the performance of 95% of venture funds. Business Insider has recognized him as one of the Top 100 global seed investors , and his perspectives are published regularly in Crunchbase News and other leading publications. payload.text: Numeracle has raised $28 million from Edison Partners to help businesses whose calls are incorrectly labeled as spam or blocked by phone carriers, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively. The McLean, Virginia-based company verifies businesses and links their identities to the phone numbers they use to contact customers. It shares that information with the systems carriers use to screen calls and works to remove incorrect labels. Rebekah Johnson, founder and CEO of Numericle. (Courtesy photo) The financing brings Numeracle’s total funding to $34.8 million since its 2018 inception. That total includes a $6.8 million Series A raised in December 2023, founder and CEO Rebekah Johnson told Crunchbase News in an interview. Edison was the sole investor in the new round. Numeracle declined to disclose its valuation. The company says it has roughly 4,000 business customers and about 85 employees. It became profitable this year, sooner than Johnson had expected. Numeracle plans to use its new capital to hire and expand internationally. The company also plans to adapt its business verification tools for use beyond phone calls. For example, Johnson said the company is eyeing messaging, chat apps, marketplaces and AI agents. Its expansion comes as businesses simultaneously face two related problems. For one,  fraudsters are increasingly impersonating them. Meanwhile, call-screening systems can prevent their own calls from reaching customers. For example, that could mean a patient ignoring a call from a hospital about an upcoming procedure. For a bank, it could mean a customer declining a legitimate call because the phone displays a fraud warning. Numeracle charges an annual subscription to monitor and address incorrect spam labels. Customers can also pay a per-call fee to display their business name, logo and reason for calling on a recipient’s phone. From a regulatory warning to a company Johnson, an engineer who previously worked in regulatory compliance at telecom provider West , said she recognized the problem while participating in the Federal Communications Commission ’s Robocall Strike Force in 2016. She warned carriers that their efforts to identify unwanted calls would also affect legitimate businesses because the screening systems lacked information about who was calling. About three months later, she said, a carrier’s federal regulatory counsel called her while she was in her parents’ kitchen. “Everything you said was going to happen is happening. What do we do?” she recalled him asking. Johnson said that conversation prompted her to start Numeracle. She was a newly single mother who had lost her job and used her life savings to start the business. Living on a farm in Grand Bay, Alabama, without internet access, she worked from cafes. “When you need to feed your children and provide a roof over their head, you’re going to count every penny,” Johnson said. That experience shaped her spending decisions as Numeracle grew, she said. The company operated for several years before raising its Series A. Johnson said about 90% of Numeracle’s sales inquiries come through unpaid inbound channels. With the new funding, she plans to spend more on marketing to specific industries, including healthcare. The company’s customers also include businesses in financial services, home services and higher education, as well as government organizations and charities. Johnson declined to identify individual customers. Verifying increasingly convincing fakes Numeracle first checks that a business is real and does what it claims. Once it passes those checks, the company links it to the phone numbers it uses and shares that information with the systems carriers use to flag or block calls. Other companies can also pay Numeracle to run those checks on businesses they’re considering taking on as customers. A business call from Numeracle, delivered with name, logo, and reason for calling. (Photo courtesy of Numeracle) Johnson said Numeracle built its own verification tools because existing services weren’t thorough enough. Fraudsters have an incentive to get through: If Numeracle approves them, their calls are less likely to be flagged as spam. AI has made it more difficult to tell which businesses are real, she said. Numeracle has encountered fake companies with state registrations, employer identification numbers and supposed employees who have active LinkedIn profiles. “The scary part for me isn’t necessarily the AI voices,” Johnson said. “It’s actually AI-built businesses.” She said Numeracle uses AI to help identify those fabrications, though she declined to describe the methods in detail. Numeracle currently operates in the United States. Johnson said interest from Europe has prompted it to move forward with its international expansion plans, with some of the new funding going toward that effort. The broader question for the company is whether businesses will pay to use its verification services across other forms of communication. For now, its business centers on a more immediate problem — helping customers recognize a legitimate phone call. Investor POV: ‘Doing more with less’ For Lenard Marcus , a general partner at Edison Partners, Johnson’s telecom and engineering experience was one major reason to invest. In an interview with Crunchbase News, he said her industry knowledge helped her build both the product and relationships with companies that could bring it to customers. He was also drawn to how much Numeracle had accomplished with relatively little funding, describing Johnson as “someone who was frankly doing more with less.” Customer interviews helped make the case. Marcus recalled one contact center operator who said Numeracle had increased the number of calls answered from 19,000 to 22,000 out of 40,000 calls a month. For businesses trying to reach prospective customers, that increase in conversations could lead to more sales. Marcus also believes that Johnson’s years in telecom give Numeracle an advantage over newer competitors. In addition to understanding how the different parts of the industry work together, Johnson has used those relationships to get Numeracle in front of large companies, he said. “She’s sales. She’s engineering, and she’s just a very, very good leader,” Marcus added. Looking ahead, the investor also sees demand across healthcare, retail, home services and finance, with AI making impersonation more prevalent. “This is a communications problem, not one for one industry,” he said. title: The Invisible Graph: How Companies Grow Revenue And Still Lose Value
summary: I got off the phone with a potential client whose company is doing great. payload.text: I got off the phone with a potential client whose company is doing great. The client, however, is not even thinking of selling the company as they see future growth over the next couple of years that they wish to materialize in order to get a larger exit. The conversation prompted me to consider something I believe many entrepreneurs miss, and it’s this: Revenue can rise while enterprise value falls. When revenue and value move in opposite directions Founders and boards routinely track revenue and profitability over time. But another graph deserves equal attention: enterprise value. Its trajectory can turn downward while the operating numbers continue improving, with significant implications for M&A timing. Consider a hypothetical SaaS company generating $15 million in annual recurring revenue, valued at 6x ARR. Its implied enterprise value is $90 million. Two years later, ARR reaches $20 million, but the multiple falls to 3.5x revenue. Enterprise value drops to $70 million. Revenue increased 33%, while value declined 22%. These are only illustrative assumptions to demonstrate how multiple compression can overshadow operating growth. For a founder postponing a sale until the next revenue milestone, the practical implication is clear: Reaching that milestone may still produce a smaller exit. Qualitative, absolute and relative factors The revenue multiplier reflects several dimensions that evolve differently. Qualitative factors include management quality, founder dependence, competitive intensity, product differentiation and strategic relevance to buyers. Absolute financial measures include revenue, EBITDA and cash flow. Relative performance measures include growth, margins, net revenue retention and gross revenue retention. Although retention metrics are expressed as percentages, their importance lies in what they reveal about customer durability and expansion. Buyers assess these measures together and compare them with relevant peers. As companies mature, their absolute results can improve while their growth rates weaken. Meanwhile, stronger profitability, better retention or deeper management capabilities may support a higher multiplier. The valuation outcome depends on the combined effect. Boards should therefore ask which characteristics will improve over the next year, which could deteriorate and how buyers might price those changes. M&A preparation should begin while you are winning A sale requires preparation, buyer engagement, negotiation and diligence, during which buyers continually reassess performance and forecasts. Waiting until a slowdown becomes visible can weaken negotiating leverage and raise questions about management’s projections. Strategic buyer demand also follows its own timetable. A buyer may place substantial value on acquiring a particular technology, customer base or geographic presence today. That interest can diminish after an internal product launch, a competing acquisition or a budget change. Waiting can still create considerable value when additional scale attracts more buyers, profitability improves or concentration falls. Boards can make that case tangible by reviewing estimated enterprise value alongside the operating plan, using scenarios in which revenue grows while the multiple holds, expands or contracts. They should also consider how debt, cash, dilution, liquidation preferences and transaction terms affect shareholder proceeds. Nobody can reliably identify the valuation peak in advance. However, every decision to delay a sale embeds a view about future valuation. That view deserves its own graph. Itay Sagie , a guest contributor to Crunchbase News, is a seasoned lecturer and strategic adviser to startups and investors, specializing in strategy, growth and M&A. You can connect with him on LinkedIn for further insights and discussions. Related Crunchbase query: Global M&A In 2026 For Venture-Backed Companies Illustration: Dom Guzman

payload.text: Editor’s note: The following is the latest profile in a series of articles about startup founders from non-technical backgrounds who have launched successful venture-backed companies. Read the previous interviews in the series including with MagicSchool AI founder Adeel Khan here , Trunk Tools founder Sarah Buchner here , Tabs founder Ali Hussain here , Craft founder Ilya Levtov here , GC AI founder Cecilia Ziniti here , Incredible Health co-founder Iman Abuzeid here , and Hilt founder William “Will” Cielen here . Lilly Chen was 16 and had been repeatedly hospitalized for Graves’ disease when her mother suggested they move to China and become monks. Frustrated with the care her daughter was receiving through Medicaid, she wanted to try something different. Lilly Chen, co-founder and CEO of FSH Technologies. (Courtesy photo) Chen left high school and spent about two years as a monk, ordained in the United States before spending several months at a monastery in China. She meditated, reread the same books, and gradually felt well enough to consider returning to school. She went on to enter Colorado College without a high school diploma, briefly play video games professionally, and become an engineer at Facebook . When she quit that job, she didn’t have a startup idea. She just wanted to find work she believed in. That mission eventually led her to FSH (pronounced “fish) Technologies ,” a Philadelphia-based company that’s building software for some of the government’s least glamorous tasks, including administering school food services and managing public records. After her brief stint at a large tech company, Chen realized she wanted to tackle the everyday problems that make people’s lives harder, even if solving them wouldn’t generate much excitement in Silicon Valley. “What does it actually take to solve the really unsexy, boring stuff?” she remembers asking herself. A different route to college Before Chen was thinking about government software, she was trying to get well enough to return to school. At the monastery in China, she meditated, ate food grown on-site or brought by nearby villagers, and lived without internet access. She continued taking thyroid medication and said her health became more manageable during that period. She also read. A lot. With no nearby place to buy books, she reread the ones she had brought, finding different places around the monastery to sit with them. Her attachment to those books prompted a conversation with a fellow monk who asked what she enjoyed about reading and where she might find more books. The discussion eventually turned to colleges, and why she wasn’t attending one. Chen explained her health problems. He observed that she seemed well. She realized she was. So Chen returned to the U.S., homeschooled herself and enrolled at Colorado College without having earned a high school diploma. She turned 20 during her freshman year and graduated in 2019 with a double major in mathematics and economics. While she was in college, Chen briefly played Dota 2 professionally. She also played against OpenAI ’s game-playing bots, an early encounter with AI technology she would later help support as an engineer. After an initial job in Boston, she joined Facebook, where she built infrastructure used to train AI models. Leaving without a startup idea Then on Jan. 6, 2021, Chen was attending a remote company all-hands meeting while watching coverage of the attack on the U.S. Capitol on another screen. Her concerns about Facebook’s role in enabling the organization of violence made her question whether she could continue working there. “I realized that I couldn’t work for Big Tech anymore,” she recalls. She quit shortly afterward. To figure out her next move, she returned to the sort of questions she had encountered as a monk. What made her happy? What mattered to her? What was she good at? Programming remained her most concrete skill. She just needed to figure out where to apply it. An introduction through Envision , a student-run accelerator focused on nontraditional founders, connected her with Contrary , a venture firm that has backed the likes of Ramp and Anduril Industries . The firm wrote Chen her first check in 2021, before she had even settled on the business that would become FSH. Although she didn’t have a developed company pitch, Chen’s earnest explanation of what motivated her and her passion for solving a meaningful problem won investors over. That investment gave her room to experiment, she said. FSH took shape into what it is today in 2024. The Contrary investor who first backed her, Jason Chen , has since joined the company as its chief operating officer. The company has raised $25 million in total funding, including a recent $20 million Series A that Chen said came together in about a week. Participants in that raise included Lachy Groom , General Catalyst , Ramp, Scribble Ventures , Operator Partners , Basis Set Ventures . Contrary also led its seed financing. Finding the problem beneath the paperwork Ultimately, Chen landed on government software because in her view, it had the potential to solve many consequential problems that attracted relatively little excitement. For example, permits, licenses, grant applications and other administrative processes can be slow for reasons that extend beyond an outdated interface, Chen noted. Information may exist in separate departments. Updating a website may require approvals from multiple stakeholders including policymakers, communications staff and an IT team. Putting a chatbot on top of that system, Chen argues, leaves much of the underlying problem unresolved. Her approach to solving some of the problems that exist within governments draws on an exchange she had years earlier at the monastery, where one of her chores was feeding koi. The head monk would periodically ask her if she thought she was the fish or the pond? Initially, Chen didn’t understand what he was asking. But he kept returning to the question, and she began thinking about it. Eventually, she picked a fish she thought resembled her: one that stayed out of fights, swam with the group and occasionally ventured off on its own. The head monk’s response was, “You’re the pond, not the fish.” Chen viewed the exchange as a lesson in looking beyond individual pieces to understand how a whole system works. Looking at government software, she believed that it meant examining why information is scattered or processes are slow before deciding what technology to build. One early area for FSH has been K-12 food services, where administrators must perform tasks such as coordinating meal planning, nutritional information and reimbursement requirements. Another is records and archive management, including the paper documents that can still require residents to visit a government office to retrieve them. FSH does use AI for tasks such as optical character recognition, translation and natural-language search. But, Chen said, the company treats it as a tool within its software, rather than relying on a chatbot or an AI agent to handle an entire process. Government sales have required patience. The company generated less than $100,000 in revenue in its first year, Chen said, reflecting the time it takes to win contracts. At the time of this interview, FSH had roughly eight or nine employees, with additional offers outstanding. Thinking slowly, moving quickly Chen’s time as a monk has also influenced how she runs the company. She admits she is skeptical of startup culture that treats sleeping in the office or working extremely long hours as evidence of commitment or a badge of pride. Rather, Chen views some of that behavior as performative, especially when it comes at the expense of the rest that she believes people need to work effectively. Her preferred motto to the team is, “Slow is smooth and smooth is fast.” “We think slowly about a lot of things, and then we do things quickly,” she said. Chen believes it’s crucial to first understand the people, departments and procedures behind a government service before trying to improve it. Looking back, Chen also credits her success to finding people willing to back someone whose experience didn’t resemble the usual résumé. That includes the college that admitted her without a high school diploma and an investor who wrote a check before she had settled on a company idea. “You definitely end up finding your own way if you just stick to being weird,” she said. In the U.S., billion-dollar rounds have also been raised this year by companies including Travis Kalanick ’s Los Angeles-based Atoms — which includes its ghost kitchen business, and divisions for robotics in mining and transport — and Pittsburgh-based Skild AI , which raised $1.4 billion for its robotics foundation model Skild Brain. Another notable round this year went to Germany-based Neura Robotics , which raised $1.4 billion for its cognitive robots, with AI and data infrastructure to build intelligence. Building out the data and model layer “We’re just seeing physical AI take off,” Ulrik Stig Hansen , co-CEO of San Francisco-based Encord , a provider of the data layer for physical AI, told Crunchbase News at its inaugural Long Horizon Physical AI Summit in San Francisco earlier this month. The compute and storage capabilities are being developed to support these systems, he noted, but building for the physical world takes time, especially compared to large language models trained on the vast troves of text on the internet. “Physical AI is very different because there is no internet of physical AI data, and so the data first has to be collected, and you have to convert it from sensor tokens to action tokens,” he said. Data sets are orders of magnitude larger for physical AI, requiring multimodal data combining vision, tactile, force and torque. “Storing all that data, curating all that data, enriching all that data, and validating that all the data works for these systems is a very expensive operation,” said Hansen. We are still in the pre-training phase of physical AI, but will soon be entering the post-training phase, he noted. More winners Around 75 robotics companies on the unicorn board have raised funding in the past three  years. Of these, more than half — 45 — joined the board just this year. Among the most highly valued robotics startups, many competing companies are building data and models, as well as varied vertical use cases in heavy industry, manufacturing, logistics and household and use cases among others. Robotics funding is surging and new unicorns are emerging, but the sector’s direction remains uncertain as companies race toward further breakthroughs over the next year. “There are a lot of companies that are raising capital, and I think a lot of them are going to win, just because there’s so many different types of applications to the physical world,” said Hansen. payload.text: In an S-1 filing today preceding what could be the largest IPO ever , Anthropic laid out extensive new details about its earnings, growth, key stakeholders and the risks it faces going forward. Clocking in at 335 pages, the document wasn’t exactly light reading. However, after a preliminary once-over, we highlight a few of the more intriguing disclosures below: Revenue growth is unusually rapid For the first half of this year, Anthropic reported revenue of $16.3 billion. That’s up 14x from the same period in 2025. Things aren’t slowing either. While the S-1 doesn’t forecast the second half of this year, Reuters has reported that Anthropic could reach a $110 billion annualized revenue run rate by year-end, citing analysts who met with company executives. But losses persist Anthropic also posted a $693 million operating income loss for the first half of 2026, down about two-thirds from last year. Its net loss for this year’s first half was $80 billion, of which about 90% stemmed from what it called a “change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFE s.” Founders hold similar stakes Each of Anthropic’s seven founders holds between 230,000 and 246,000 shares of Class A stock, per the S-1. This kind of egalitarianism seems unusual given that startup prospectuses usually show a founding CEO with a much larger relative stake compared to co-founders. The company’s co-founders include Dario Amodei , Daniela Amodei , Tom Brown , Jack Clark , Jared Kaplan , Sam McCandlish and Christopher Olah . Anthropic’s risk factors take up 93 pages of its IPO filing So, is investing in Anthropic a risky bet? Anthropic certainly seems to think so. The company’s IPO prospectus contains a staggering 93 pages of risk factors. They start at page 27 and end on page 120. Some are pretty mundane. For instance, the company is concerned that slower revenue growth could potentially constrain its ability to fund frontier AI development and attract and retain top talent. Having incurred significant debt to date, it’s worried about the ability to keep servicing those obligations while still covering operating costs. But more unusual risks, like rogue AI agents, are in there too. In one section, Antrophic notes that “future models are expected to demonstrate capabilities that could provide meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons.” Related Crunchbase query: Global IPOs For Venture-Backed Companies In 2026 Related reading: Oura Hits Pause On IPO While Anthropic’s Prospectus Reveals The Cost Of Its AI Ambitions The AI IPO Wave Is The Dot-Com Bubble’s Evil Twin. title: When Traction Becomes Personal Exposure: What The Joonko Guilty Plea Means For Founders
summary: By Kyle Jeziorski Ilit Raz , founder and former CEO of the AI startup Joonko , raised roughly $27 million after telling investors the company had customers it never had and revenue it never actually earned. When an investor later asked for proof, she sent a forged bank statement and fake purchase orders. Last month, Raz pleaded guilty to federal securities fraud . She faces a maximum of 20 years in prison. Founders raising capital must sell investors on what their companies could become. But Raz’s case illustrates the personal stakes of misrepresenting a business’ achievements, and investors are increasingly willing to take those claims to court. payload.text: By Kyle Jeziorski Ilit Raz , founder and former CEO of the AI startup Joonko , raised roughly $27 million after telling investors the company had customers it never had and revenue it never actually earned. When an investor later asked for proof, she sent a forged bank statement and fake purchase orders. Last month, Raz pleaded guilty to federal securities fraud . She faces a maximum of 20 years in prison. Founders raising capital must sell investors on what their companies could become. But Raz’s case illustrates the personal stakes of misrepresenting a business’ achievements, and investors are increasingly willing to take those claims to court. Plaintiffs filed 15 AI-related securities class actions just in the first half of 2026, nearly matching the 16 filed in all of 2025, according to Cornerstone Research . The distinction between future potential and present-day facts matters when describing customers, revenue and traction. Where ‘puffery’ crosses the line into securities fraud Kyle Jeziorski of Founder Shield. The issue isn’t whether a pitch sounds optimistic or ambitious, but whether its factual claims mislead investors. Knowingly misrepresenting metrics that matter to an investor’s decision can expose that founder to personal liability. Before presenting a pitch deck, founders should scrutinize four key areas where those distinctions can often become blurred: LOIs and pilots: Labeling soft, nonbinding letters of intent or unpaid test runs as “committed recurring revenue” or “signed enterprise contracts.” Customer counts: Presenting free pilot users or informal trial accounts as active, paying customers to inflate user growth. Traction and churn: Omitting significant customer losses in a way that makes growth claims misleading, or presenting one-time project fees as recurring revenue. Product capabilities: Presenting human-assisted workflows as fully autonomous AI systems, or claiming proprietary technology the company does not own. Legally, the question boils down to whether a misstatement or omission is material. Would a reasonable investor consider the information important when deciding to invest? Let’s be clear: An inaccurate figure doesn’t automatically establish securities fraud. But false claims about customer contracts, recurring revenue or retention can expose founders to securities-fraud claims. An ambitious forecast is one thing; a false claim about existing customers or revenue is another. The latter can expose founders personally, with no guarantee that D&O insurance will cover the fallout. Where D&O coverage may stop Founders facing investor claims typically look to directors and officers, or D&O, insurance for protection. But defending a fraud allegation isn’t the same as covering established misconduct. The policy’s wording and applicable law determine where protection ends. As part of a June 2025 court-approved settlement with Joonko, Raz reportedly agreed to abandon claims against the company’s D&O policies. Still, that doesn’t clarify whether an insurer had previously funded her legal defense or denied coverage. Three policy provisions deserve attention: The fraud exclusion: D&O policies commonly exclude losses arising from deliberate fraud, criminal conduct or improper personal profit. Allegations alone generally do not trigger those exclusions. Final adjudication: Insurers may advance defense costs while a case proceeds. A guilty plea or conviction can trigger an exclusion, but the policy wording sets the exact threshold, including whether appeals must be exhausted. Repayment provision: Some policies allow insurers to recover advanced defense costs if the claim is ultimately excluded. Founders should check whether repayment is required and under what circumstances. D&O insurance can help founders during investor disputes, but it’s not a guaranteed backstop for established fraud. Founders must understand when coverage can end and whether they’ll have to pay back the legal fees their insurer advanced. Practical steps for founders before presenting metrics Before sharing a pitch deck, create an easily accessible guide for your team that spells out your math. Specify what counts as a paying customer, how pilots and LOIs are classified, and how recurring revenue and churn are calculated. Use those definitions consistently. Team with finance and legal advisers to connect material claims to supporting records, including executed contracts, invoices, accounting data and customer-status reports. Keep projections separate from current results, and document the assumptions behind the forecasts. Don’t confuse ARR with cash collected; they do not belong in the same category. Show clearly how the company calculates recurring revenue and distinguishes it from one-time fees, pipeline opportunities and contracted commitments that haven’t gone live yet. Remember that ARR and contracted ARR are distinct metrics, not to be used interchangeably. Lastly, date the figures and update material changes before investors rely on them for decision-making. If the team can’t explain how they calculate a number or substantiate a customer claim, resolve the discrepancy before presenting your deck. Investors might buy into your vision, but regulators will look at your math. Kyle Jeziorski is the managing director of the innovation practice at The Baldwin Group , advising leaders in emerging industries on management and professional liability. He has 14 years of experience in insurance and joined the firm when it was still Founder Shield. Before that, he was on Marsh ‘s FINPRO team, covering management liability for large private and public companies. Off the clock, Jeziorski is on the golf course, in the kitchen or watching his Buffalo sports teams. Illustration: Dom Guzman

title: doomformer
summary: I Turned DOOM into a Transformer

extra.author: falperc
extra.original_title: Show HN: I Turned DOOM into a Transformer

story_text.value:
Instead of trying to run DOOM on things, I have instead decided to use DOOM (many, many, many doom games actually) to create a transformer. For a lot of the math required I essentially had to use DOOM game mechanics and voodoo dolls (DOOM is turing complete btw) and exchange them with the actual operations, essentially creating an alternative to NumPy (a 65000x slower one). Thus, I am proud to present DOOMFORMER. Here are a list of things DOOMFORMER can do :

It can classify MNIST digits, even if you write these digits on the map!

It can talk(kinda)

You can use it to make decisions, so, it can play DOOM. Yes! You can play DOOM with thousands of DOOM games now! The marine's mind can be controlled by DOOM, playing on a map generated by DOOMFORMER. Truly, the possibilities are endless, and even larger-scale training of DOOMFORMER could be done on a measly T4.

If anyone would like to help me scale this up and make crazier things, I'd love to work together.

title: Artificer by Nua
summary: Frontier robotics task evaluation in 4B parameters

extra.author: SunnyWan
extra.original_title: Show HN: Artificer by Nua: Frontier robotics task evaluation in 4B parameters

story_text.value:
We’re happy to introduce Artificer, our first robotics decision model for evaluating robot task progress and success. The problem Robot systems need feedback during training, evaluation, and deployment. An arm might grasp the right object, but place it in the wrong bin. A robot might’ve only completed part of its task before it stopped. Assessing these outcomes from video often requires manual review or brittle, handcrafted objectives. Though frontier models do well in evaluation, they are expensive and slow. Artificer is a 4B parameter model that estimates task completion and progress, at the frontier level, from a task description and video. During deployment, these estimates provide feedback to a robot controller to help decide whether to continue an attempt, retry, or move to the next task.

Know a robotics team working on task evaluation or success detection? We'd appreciate an introduction! For the robotics founders: we’d love to test Artificer on your task videos! Would love to chat more in the comments or over email! sunny@trynua.dev

title: Sunlight
summary: the camera-based infinite canvas window manager for Mac

extra.author: darindd
extra.original_title: Show HN: Sunlight – the camera-based infinite canvas window manager for Mac

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I'm Darin. You might know me from my work at Webflow (YC S13) and currently Ploy (YC P26).

Sunlight is the way I imagined the Mac working before I got my 1st-gen MacBook Air in high school (2008). I had looked at a bunch of Apple videos of Mission Control (Exposé back then) and somehow decided it worked like an infinite canvas. I even told my mom about it! I guess it stuck with me.

Windowing on the Mac is so good it's one of those "if it ain't broke don't fix it" things. And yet, it always felt lacking. So Sunlight reimagines it from first principles:

- 355"+ virtual desktop

- 120fps, fully native

- Multi-touch interactions

- Guides, grids and haptics

- Minimap

- ⌘Tab and Mission Control work as usual

- Works with your Dock, widgets and desktop

- Collision detection and magnetic windows

- Tiling and saved layouts

- Deeply customizable

- ...and much more (including agent support) coming soon

Free and open source, forever.

Launch demo (2:34): https://youtu.be/NSerIT8zRpw

title: Overtone
summary: Transcribe, correct and cut captions for any screen shape

extra.author: rvanderlinden
extra.original_title: Show HN: Overtone – Transcribe, correct and cut captions for any screen shape

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Ruud, co-founder of Lont. We turn company emails into personalized videos.

Video captions cost us manual work twice: fixing misheard words, then fixing layout, like lines ending on “the”.

Overtone uses multiple models to listen to the audio: gpt-transcribe, Azure STT, and Elevenlabs Scribe. When they return conflicting results, Overtone sends small clips to the models again, and then lets an LLM decide what was actually said.

The LLM is like a human doing a sanity check on the transcription model. Humans would easily recognize a word to be different based on context. The LLM basically does the same, using an optional context prompt + its world knowledge. Because of this the Word Error Rate (WER) on many test files is lower when using Overtone, compared to just using a model without it.

Sure, the cost is higher because we use up to 3 different STT models + an LLM, but it still removes mistakes, reducing the time needed to fix captions to a minimum, and reducing the chance you'll miss something. For us it's worth it. For ultra high volume use cases it may not be.

The rules-based cutter nicely cuts the transcript into captions that look good, depending on screen size: 16:9 is different from 9:16, and the Overtone Format we created supports any type really. Pauses become breaks, captions are grouped per speaker, and names/numbers are never spread out over multiple captions.

How to add these captions to your videos? A videojs plugin can do this automatically, so you don't burn in your captions. The plugin lets you cycle between styled captions, plain captions, and off. You can burn them into an MP4 file with overtone burn.

Quickly try it out just the cutter? Try:

  npx overtone-captions recut yoursub.srt
Transcribing audio with API keys works too. Use --dry-run to show a cost estimate before you send.

We open-sourced this first version (MIT) because we believe many people can benefit from this, especially if your captions just need to be good. There's plenty of room to improve though, so we've made it easy to help contribute to add style packs, languages, and providers/models.

You can find a demo at: https://overtone.lont.ai/

Find the code and benchmarks here: https://github.com/lonthq/overtone-captions

summary: I got tired of travel spreadsheets so I made a travel planner app

extra.author: stavros
extra.original_title: Show HN: I got tired of travel spreadsheets so I made a travel planner app

story_text.value:
Hey everyone! I couldn't find an app to organize trips that gave me all the info I wanted to schedule each stop per day, with travel times, leeway, etc, so I made Wherewhen.

The basic differentiator is that you can set various constraints (e.g. "I want to spend 2 hours in the park", or "I have a dinner reservation at 6"), and Wherewhen will automatically adjust the rest of the times to tell you when to go/leave each place, including travel.

I've tried to make it mobile-friendly but travel planning is pretty complicated and it's a bit clunky on mobile.

Feedback is appreciated!

summary: Hello HN, I've been working on a new Web engine, build around two ideas: - use formal methods from day one. - make it modular. The modularity is orientated towards the following goals: - enabling shipping anywhere, …

extra.author: polyglotfacto
extra.original_title: Show HN: A malleable and formally verified Web engine

story_text.value:
Hello HN,

I've been working on a new Web engine, build around two ideas:

- use formal methods from day one. - make it modular.

The modularity is orientated towards the following goals:

- enabling shipping anywhere, including on IOS in the EU as per Apple’s guidelines. - only write code for stuff the OS or application platform cannot do for you: keep binary size to a minimum and achieve native performance. - developer choice: bring what you want, and only build what you need.

For example you can choose a JS engine like v8 or Boa, or just bring your own. The entire graphics pipeline consists of components whose implementation can be swapped-out, with currently a relatively fast path on Mac integrating with Core Animation and a slower cross platform path.

Project is at https://github.com/gterzian/formal-web

Intro essay at: https://medium.com/@polyglot_factotum/how-i-am-building-a-we...

Please let me know what you think.

extra.author: cat-whisperer

story_text.value:
My friend and I are Neovim nerds, and every so often our Neovim setups would throw errors. What did we do? We talked to each other and solved it. It was never Neovim’s fault.

We think the same way about harnesses. If you don’t like something, you shouldn’t have to call a trillion-dollar company; you should be able to fix it yourself. If you want something custom, you shouldn’t have to keep spamming some discussion thread; you should be able to write it yourself.

And more than anything, it should be simple and fast, and your computer shouldn’t scream OOM. That’s the inspiration behind uji.

I hope you all love it!!!

title: Fabivo
summary: Furniture design from a photo to a numbered cut list

extra.author: superpapotas
extra.original_title: Show HN: Fabivo – Furniture design from a photo to a numbered cut list

story_text.value:
Hello all,

Ive been building Fabivo, a free furniture planner that runs in the browser. You sketch it simply by drawing it, (by far my favorite feature of this app), clicking for boards or just selecting some starting designs.

But what i think separates fabivo from others its the image to model ai assistant, which took me a looong time to develop and get some quirks fixed, thanks god latest models are focusing on 3d, thats been helping too!

The photo part is an image to JSON CAD harness: the model returns a parametric furniture model in mm that the app can build and edit. That harness is also what i benchmark, and honestly its the reason the app exists. I wanted to see if a photo could turn into a plan i could take to the saw.

Also finetuned some image models and found interesting stuff, that was a first. My intention was to basically reuse the drawing feature to convert a 2d line sketch from image models like gpt image / nano banana to my parametric model, which "worked", and was actually thinking of using that for prod, but then cheaper/better models at 3d launched, but anyways, i learned a lot!

Im getting better performance from my harness than from plain 3js, tho this is anecdotally and havent actually benchmarked it...

Happy to answer anything, especially about the harness or the cut order.

edit: Adding the numbers, missed them.

17 photos of real furniture, three models, same harness, medium reasoning, same tools. Scored on how close the returned structure and boards are to the gold model, so its my own set. (tho i have a hard time making a good scoring metric... just usually go by look!)

Model (medium reasoning) Avg. time / photo Avg. input tokens / photo Avg. output tokens / photo Avg. tool calls / photo GPT-6.1 Terra 9.5 s 30,409 632 1.06 Claude Sonnet 5.5 13.6 s 50,167 1,592 1.18 Claude Haiku 5.5 34.9 s 66,786 6,658 2.35

Terra was both cheaper per photo and the most consistent to my likings. Sonnet was close on quality, Haiku needed way more tool calls to get there.

title: I built a tool that finds reliability bugs in your code
summary: Hey HN, I’m Abhishek. I'm building Opslane, a tool that finds reliability issues in your code. On every PR, it spins up your entire app and then tries to find weak spots that would break in production. Demo: https:&…

extra.author: aray07
extra.original_title: Show HN: I built a tool that finds reliability bugs in your code

story_text.value:
Hey HN,

I’m Abhishek. I'm building Opslane, a tool that finds reliability issues in your code. On every PR, it spins up your entire app and then tries to find weak spots that would break in production.

Demo: https://youtu.be/47phxkdh6f0

Example: We tested Opslane on Lago (open-source billing) and found a bug where customers get double charged. Opslane made Stripe take the money and then return a 500. Lago marked the payment failed. A retry from the dashboard charged the customer again. https://github.com/getlago/lago-api/issues/6903

Why I built this

I used to work on reliability at Robinhood. We used to run chaos testing in our staging environments: inject faults in various parts of the system and see what breaks. We found issues like Kafka or Redis being unavailable for a few seconds could take the whole app down.

But that kind of testing was expensive. It needed a well maintained staging environment. Engineers needed to know what to test. Most teams never actually did it.

Over the last year, coding agents have gone writing some of my code to almost all my code now. Teams are shipping way more code than they were 6 months ago.

Code review tools read the diff, but a lot of reliability bugs aren't in the diff. They're in how your code behaves when Stripe, Redis or the network misbehaves. And e2e tests usually mock those services out and test the happy path.

Agents have made this type of testing a lot cheaper. And we will see more of this (kinda like security scanning / testing)

How it works

A full copy of your app per PR: Postgres, Redis, Kafka, SQS, S3.

Working copies of your third-party dependencies: Stripe, Slack, Gmail and more. Traffic goes through our proxy, which lets us inject failures.

The agent picks what to test: It reads every PR and writes down invariants that need to hold (for e.g. a customer should never be charged twice). It then injects faults likely to break the invariants.

Bugs we've found

We ran Opslane on some popular open-source apps and here are some of the bugs we have found:

1/ Twenty: deleting a workspace while Stripe is failing locks everyone out, and billing keeps going. Twenty merged a fix. (https://github.com/twentyhq/twenty/issues/28043)

2/ Dub: a restart in the middle of a payout paid a partner $240 for $120 owed. (https://github.com/dubinc/dub.link/issues/4707)

Full list: opslane.com/open-source

Opslane is pretty early - we have a couple of early customers. We have found bugs in their system that their other code review tools missed.

Would love to get feedback from folks and how they are seeing the reliability of their systems evolve over time with agents.

story_text.value:
The linked repo is 100% vibe coded, but it was built on a handful of principles:

- Most tax software derives trust from the party who maintains it (e.g. Intuit, the IRS, etc.)

- Vibe coded software lacks this trustworthiness.

- Therefore any formalization should build in verifiability and mechanisms that make it possible for users/maintainers to trace claims/interpretations back to authoritative source documents.

It's very much a back-burner passive project right now (do not use this for anything real!), but I feel strongly that something like this ought to exist for the public good. I built it to get a sense of what the shape of what such a thing might be.

title: OpenTaxRate
summary: open-source US sales tax rates by street address

extra.author: winxton
extra.original_title: Show HN: OpenTaxRate – open-source US sales tax rates by street address

story_text.value:
I built this because I tried many sales tax APIs and the problems were: a) the rates were a black box with no source attached b) lookups resolved by ZIP code.

ZIP codes are postal routes, not tax jurisdictions. Stripe's Tax team wrote a good post on this [1]: two houses in Drexel, MO share a city, a ZIP, and nearly a house number, but sit in different counties with different rates. If your lookup key is the ZIP, you are wrong on those addresses, even when the rate table is accurate.

OpenTaxRate resolves the street address instead: - SST member states (24): the quarterly rate + boundary files, street ranges and ZIP+4, not just the rate tables - Non-SST states: a custom adapter for each state, using its DOR's own published tables and boundary files (TX Comptroller, FL DR-15DSS, ALDOR, IDOR, NY Pub 718, California via CDTFA's lookup, etc) - Census TIGER for geometry

I tried with multiple open source geocoders you can self-host: Nominatim, Photon and Pelias, as well as proprietary ones (HERE, Geocodio, Mapbox, Google). Proprietary ones have higher accuracy, ~99.3% correct vs. 97.1% with just open source.

For comparison: Avalara AvaTax 99.6%, TaxJar 98.2%. Public benchmark set are in the repo and at opentaxrate.com/benchmarks.

Rates are just one part of sales tax, but also there's a ton of work in maintaining it as rules change. It doesn't handle exemptions, holidays, and caps.

It returns the rate, plus the state's own location and jurisdiction codes for the address, resolved to the address, with its official source attached. MIT licensed, you can self-host with Postgres + PostGIS.

[1]: https://stripe.dev/blog/how-we-built-it-jurisdiction-resolut...

title: nodal-context
summary: Interview your analysts instead of auto-generating a semantic layer

extra.author: ronpotok
extra.original_title: Show HN: Interview your analysts instead of auto-generating a semantic layer

story_text.value:
I’ve spent the last year building context for AI analysts in the mid-market. I’ve open sourced a library from my learnings, along the same principles of the Matt Pocock skills.

Principles:

* Claude / Codex / Cursor etc are great data agents - you just need context to enable them to answer business questions correctly.

* Much of the important context lives in analysts heads'

* Context must be maintainable (short, human readable - markdown and yaml)

* Added context should be load bearing, not repeat of information that is available in another source of truth - and evaluations prove the value of the context

* Companies should own their own context, and must be shareable with any model

* Context should be version controlled (and github works as a context store).

What the library does:

* Performs an interview with your analysts (context-interview skill), one domain at a time, similar to what I have done as a consultant. The interview is informed by your query logs.

* The AI develops evaluation questions at the same time as building the context - and at the end of each domain interview asks you to run an evaluation with and without the context. The evaluation will actually check the results against your dashboards if you allow it. We have shown increases in accuracy from 87% to 95% by adding this context in our imaginary open-source company, Shorelane.

* Provides a set of skills to use the context that follow best practices for self service analytics:

  * Write a plain english plan for the business user to approve

  * Execute the plan

  * Verify that the execution followed the plan, and provide a simple uncertainty score. 

  * Enable a adversarial review of the answer if their are doubts.
What you get:

Context repo written in markdown and yaml after you finish the interview. We use a single github repo, divided into domains. The interview can be shared and restarted by checking in/out of github.

A set of skills to share with your business team

Optional: We offer a fast MCP server to serve the Github-based context to your team.

title: Simantic (YC F26)
summary: Firmware Simulation for AI Agents

extra.author: shong0504
extra.original_title: Launch HN: Simantic (YC F26) – Firmware Simulation for AI Agents

story_text.value:
Hi HN, we're Ahnaf and Seungmin from Simantic (https://simantic.com). We are building the simulation layer that lets engineers and AI agents test and validate firmware without hardware.

Before Simantic, we were ex-firmware engineers at companies like Neuralink and Tesla. We’ve worked on some of the coolest projects, like the Cybertruck and Roadster, back when they were still early prototypes.

We started working on firmware back when ChatGPT didn’t exist yet, but over the years, we saw how much of the engineering and development work has been automated as the frontier models improved to this point. In software, AI can run and test code inside your computer in a matter of seconds. But as firmware engineers, we didn’t have that luxury. An AI agent can write firmware in seconds, but in order to test it, we had to flash a physical board, then manually run tests using expensive and clunky tools with software made over a decade ago.

To speed up the validation loop, we built the simulation layer that lets AI agents test the firmware and make decisions based on evidence, instead of waiting for the engineer to run tests for them. We used to spend hours testing our firmware manually on devboards, but now we use our own simulation to validate firmware in seconds.

What we offer: - Virtual devboards you can program and run with a single API call, without leaving your terminal. - An AI code reviewer for firmware, that makes informed decisions based on evidence, using our simulation as a verification engine. - A CI/CD pipeline for your hardware projects that validates your firmware against a simulated version of the microcontroller on every commit.

Here is a demo of our simulation used in an AI code review session: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kBK1ZjGWWbQ

Our users are using Simantic for bare-metal and RTOS development for applications like flight controllers, electric vehicles, robotics, and satellites. For safety critical systems like avionics and automotives, a robust simulation system is incredibly important, because every change in the firmware puts a human life at stake, especially for machines that cost hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars.

We recently helped an early stage space startup building satellites, to test their firmware on hardware that they don't yet have. Even the development modules for those satellites costs over $100k, and we helped them do that at just a hundredth of the cost and time.

Early on in our journey, we established our idea to make better simulation but didn’t have a clear idea of how we would do it, we considered developing our software around open source emulation frameworks like Renode (https://github.com/renode/renode) and QEMU (https://www.qemu.org/), because they were tools already used within the firmware industry. We built our MVP that was essentially a wrapper around Renode, but we quickly realized there were a lot of limitations to doing this.

1. We were bottlenecked by the development speed of Renode themselves. We tried making contributions on Github to fix issues we came across, but the speed in which we could merge our features in was not fast enough for a startup like us trying to move fast.

2. Renode is built using Dotnet, and it was proving itself to be slower than we would have liked. Renode was released in 2017, which was when all code was still being written by hand, so I think it made sense looking back, but there were limitations because of the language itself.

3. The open source tools were bloated, with features that we would never use. Yes, there were a breadth of features, but we had a lot of things we had to work around just because we couldn’t remove or change them. Users were complaining about simulation accuracy. Renode is an emulator at the core, but our users, especially those who are building systems where timing accuracy is crucial did not find the accuracy good enough to validate their firmware.

Because of these issues, we made our own simulation engine from scratch, fully written in Rust.

- Our simulation is focused on accuracy. Open source frameworks often focus on expandability and developer experience, which means there were a lot of tradeoffs made to prioritize a breadth of models rather than going deep into a set of select models.

- We have our own hardware validation rigs running 24/7 to ensure our simulation models are as close to real world hardware as possible, and any gaps are detected and fixed as soon as we can. It currently looks like devboards connected to a Saleae Logic MSO and a SWD bus, controlled by a Linux PC, running Claude 24/7 just finding these gaps.

Our cloud-hosted simulator is available to use right now! We also provide a native binary with our developer plan licenses that let you run your firmware on your machines locally without any limitations.

Check it out at https://simantic.com/cloud-sim, and you can start using our AI firmware reviewer bot in your own Github repos here: https://simantic.com/dashboard/simantic-bot.

We currently have support for some models of the STM32F0, F4, H7 series MCUs, ESP32-S3/C3, and RP2040, but we’re constantly working to release new models every week, and improve our existing ones.

Thank you, and if you have any questions, feel free to send us an email at founders@simantic.dev

title: huggingface/transformers: v5.22.0: Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk)
summary: ## New Models ### Mistral Large 4 (Le Chonk) Mistral Large 4 is Mistral's largest and most capable model to date: a 1 trillion-parameter natively multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model with 49 billion active parameters per token (52 billion including embeddings and output layers), trained from scratch on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral's own datacenters in Europe. Mistral Large 4 unifies instruction following, reasoning, coding, and agentic workflows in a single set of weights. While a generalist model, it shows especially good performance on workloads such as cybersecurity, finance, and law, and it surpasses frontier closed models on visual grounding. It is natively fluent in 160+ languages, including every official language of the European Union. #### Key Features Mistral Large 4 includes the following architectural choices: - **~1T total / ~52B active parameters**: granular Mixture-of-Experts with 128 routed experts (4 active per token) and 1 shared expert. - **1M context length**, for long-context workloads. - **Multimodal input**: accepts text and image input, with text output. Pixtral-style vision encoder trained to handle variable image sizes and aspect ratios. - **Instruct and Reasoning functionalities** with function calls, reasoning effort configurable per request. Mistral Large 4 offers the following capabilities: - **Reasoning Mode**: three reasoning efforts — `low`, `medium`, `high` (default) — so the same model can answer a quick chat reply or work through a complex agentic run. - **Vision**: analyzes images, charts, technical drawings, and documents, with state-of-the-art visual grounding among open weights. - **Multilingual**: natively fluent in 160+ languages, including all official languages of the European Union. - **System Prompt**: strong adherence and support for system prompts. - **Agentic**: native function calling, JSON output, and strict JSON schema enforcement. - **Cybersecurity**: state of the art among open-weight models for security work, while refusing malicious requests. - **Large Context Window**: supports a 1M context window. The model is released under the [**Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License**](https://huggingface.co/mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B/blob/main/LICENSE): a modified version of the MIT license, for both commercial and non-commercial use — operating a Model-as-a-Service business requires a separate commercial license with Mistral. #### Recommended Settings - **Reasoning Effort**: - `'low'` / `'medium'` / `'high'` — default is `'high'`. - Use `reasoning_effort="high"` for complex prompts and agentic usage, `'low'` for fast chat replies and `'medium'` for day to day usage. - **Sampling**: for all reasoning efforts, we recommend the following sampling parameters: - `temperature=1.0` - `top_p=0.95` - **System Prompt**: define a clear environment and use case, including guidance on how to effectively leverage tools in agentic systems. - **Tools**: keep the set of tools well-defined and limit their number to the minimum required for the use case. - **Context**: the checkpoint supports a 1M context window. ## Breaking changes * 🚨 Separate EP logic into its own file (#49679) by @3outeille ## Quantization FP8 quantized models can now be used for adapter training (such as LoRA with PEFT). Backward passes were added to the dense and grouped FP8 matmuls, and `is_trainable` is now `True`. Backward also dequantizes experts in chunks and skips autograd at inference, which cuts peak memory in the MoE layer backward from about 28.9 GiB to 2.8 GiB at 8k tokens. Separately, the AMD CI image now install * FP8 backward: chunked expert dequant, skip autograd.Function at inference (#50117) by @ArthurZucker in [#50117] * Train adapters on top of FP8 weights (#50031) by @qgallouedec in [#50031] * [AMD CI] Install onnxscript, bitsandbytes and peft in the AMD image (#50046) by @Abdennacer-Badaoui in [#50046] ## Bugfixes and improvements * Processor title: ggerganov/llama.cpp: v0.8.0
summary:
## Overview

This release adds the LiquidAI LFM3 family (text, vision, audio and omni) together with a new experimental streaming-audio API in `mtmd`, and wires realtime audio in and out of the server through the new `/v1/realtime` and `/tts` endpoints. A batch of new architectures landed: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, SenseNova U1, Beam, Kolibri-1, Flint, Muse Spark, Granite Switch Decision, plus decision/embedding models from LiquidAI, Baidu and NVIDIA. The core got sparse-attention (QSA/DSA) reworked onto a fused masking op, a 50/50 SLRU cache for host-resident MoE experts, and cleaner `no_alloc` memory handling; the server got router memory-management and tool-calling improvements; the UI can now browse and download models straight from HF Hub, search conversations and compact them. Finally, `ggml` was bumped to v0.28.0, bringing `GGML_OP_TOP_K_MASK`, `-1` expert-index semantics and large backend performance work (CUDA chunked graph launches, SYCL graph replay, OpenCL Q2_K/Q3_K, Hexagon HTP rework, KleidiAI SVE kernels).

### Highlights

- LFM3 family: LFM3-1.7B (text) and LFM3-VL-2B (vision), verified against the reference HF implementation [llama/31252](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31252)
- LFM3-Audio-2B and LFM3-Omni-2B: ASR, TTS and voice chat from a single model, with streaming audio input and output [llama/31257](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31257)

### API changes

- DRY sampler: new `LLAMA_DRY_MAX_SEQ_BREAKERS` (64) caps distinct sequence breakers, each costing `O(n_vocab)` at init [llama/31035](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31035)
- `mtmd`: new experimental `mtmd_audio_stream` API turning PCM fed as it arrives into decoder-ready embedding rows [llama/30629](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30629)
- `mtmd`: audio generation is now stateful - `mtmd_gen_state` replaces the raw `state_data` buffers of the audio gen API [llama/30902](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30902)
- `mtmd`: `mtmd_caps` gained `gen_audio`; new TTS types `SOPRANO` and `LFM3A`; repetition penalty for sampled codes [llama/28607](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28607) [llama/31257](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31257)
- `mtmd_helper_get_capabilities()` to query the capabilities of an mmproj file from helper code [llama/31183](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31183)
- Server: new `/v1/realtime` endpoint implementing the OpenAI realtime protocol for conversation and transcription [llama/31269](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31269) [llama/30636](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30636)
- Server: new `POST /tts` endpoint for text-to-speech models [llama/26603](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26603)
- Server: reasoning effort levels of the chat template are exposed and selectable via the API [llama/31271](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31271)
- Chat API: support for deferred tools and `tool_reference` content parts [llama/31256](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31256)
- CLI: `--model` or `-hf` is now required [llama/31242](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31242)

### New models

- LiquidAI LFM3-1.7B, LFM3-VL-2B, LFM3-Audio-2B, LFM3-Omni-2B [llama/31252](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31252) [llama/31257](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31257)
- LiquidAI d1-2B and d1-omni-2B decision models [llama/31275](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31275)
- DeepSeek V4.1 Flash [llama/31086](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31086)
- SenseNova U1 [llama/28919](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28919)
- Beam (Reflection) [llama/30670](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30670)
- Kolibri-1 (Aleph-Alpha) [llama/30673](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30673)
- Flint [llama/30928](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30928)
- Muse Spark Open (text, vision and audio) [llama/30616](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30616)
- Granite Switch Decision, including the 256-way decision head [llama/30676](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30676) [llama/30693](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30693)
- Nemotron-3(.5)-Embed, with non-standard GQA and BPE tokenizer support [llama/30877](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30877) [llama/23343](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/23343)
- H2O-Lightning-4B decision model [llama/30361](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30361)
- MiniCPM-OCR 1.0 and MiniCPM-OCR-Jev [llama/30979](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30979) [llama/30980](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30980)
- Soprano TTS [llama/28607](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/28607)
- LFM2 short-conv and FFN blocks moved into a shared LFM base reused by newer LFM models [llama/30874](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30874)

### Core changes

- MoE experts kept in host memory now use a 50/50 SLRU cache instead of a plain LRU cache [llama/30637](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30637)
- Sparse attention: fused QSA mask op, QSA/DSA selection built without `kq_mask`, k-pool views shared between layers [llama/30640](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30640) [llama/31009](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31009) [llama/30965](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30965) [llama/31243](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31243) [llama/30613](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30613)
- MoE: amax rescaling enabled for `laguna`, and `-sm tensor` denied on arches that use it [llama/31147](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31147) [llama/31081](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31081)
- Memory: `no_alloc` respected in all memory caches, moved out of `llama_hparams`, obsolete `n_pad` dropped [llama/31087](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31087) [llama/31141](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31141) [llama/31200](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31200)
- Vocabulary loading optimized; `d2t` placed next to its `set_rows` use so it can stay on the GPU [llama/30679](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30679) [llama/30912](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30912)
- Tokenizer: new `clean_spaces` and metaspace prepend-scheme GGUF keys, hybrid DNA tokenizer fixes [llama/30940](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30940) [llama/30825](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30825)
- Tokenizer: Tekken pre-tokenizer for Pixtral, `\p{M}` in Tekken/GPT-4o lookaheads, Nemotron-3.5-Embed tokenization fix [llama/30960](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30960) [llama/30845](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30845) [llama/30974](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30974)
- Grammar: recursion depth limited (and enforced) to prevent stack overflow; deep JSON rejected before walking it [llama/29755](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29755) [llama/31153](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31153) [llama/30242](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30242)
- Qwen: merge tensors on convert, 2D output reshape, Qwen3 bidirectional attention and `dense_2` output projection [llama/31028](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31028) [llama/30823](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30823) [llama/30607](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30607)
- Speculative decoding: persist the dynamic ngram cache, probabilistic DFlash2 drafts, optional DFlash FC input scale [llama/22055](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/22055) [llama/30663](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30663) [llama/30945](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30945) [llama/30927](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30927)
- LoRA: support for `prism.hadamard` folded weights [llama/30910](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30910)
- Tensor parallel: `stepfun` and `laguna` now support 4-10 GPUs [llama/24554](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24554)
- GGUF tools reject truncated tensor data in `split`, `export-lora` and `merge` [llama/30497](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/30497) [llama/31044](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31044)

- Discover and download models directly from HF Hub, with org-less models listed first [llama/29584](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29584) [llama/31215](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/31215)

### ggml changes

- Bumped from v0.27.0 to [ggml v0.28.0](https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/releases/tag/v0.28.0)
- New `GGML_OP_TOP_K_MASK` fused sparse-attention mask, plus accessors for the precision configured on a compute node
- `-1` is now a valid expert index in `MUL_MAT_ID`/`ADD_ID`: the slot is skipped and the output row zeroed
- `SCALE` accepts non-contiguous row views; `SUM` accepts non-contiguous inputs on CPU, CUDA, Vulkan and WebGPU
- Backends: fused MoE top-k and gate/up+GLU with chunked graph launches on CUDA, graph record/replay on SYCL
- Backends: Q2_K/Q3_K weights and a lightning indexer on OpenCL, subgroup reductions and `src1` precision on Vulkan
- More: restructured Hexagon HTP backend, flash attention on ZDNN, Q2_0 on WebGPU, KleidiAI SVE GEMV/GEMM kernels
